items.a03-h: Eli Raz, Man of the Desert and the Dead Sea
items.a03-p002: I first met Eli some time in the late 1970s, when I was appointed director of the Sde Boker Field School and Eli was nearing the end of his years at the Ein Gedi Field School. Until then he had taught the geology part of the guides' courses of the Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel, and I stepped into his shoes.
items.a03-p003: In the research for his master's thesis, Eli unlocked one of the secrets (raz) of the geology of the Judean Desert, a riddle that until then had gone unexplained: he put forward a model for the development of the dolomite plates of the Judean Desert, and we used that model in our own guiding in the area.
items.a03-p004: In 1989 Eli asked me to join his team in a cross-Negev motor navigation contest, the "Rally to the Negev". I may confess that the offer flattered me very much. For two or three days we ploughed along the dusty tracks of the Negev, each of us showing off his intimate knowledge of the secrets (raz) of the desert.
items.a03-p005: In the early 2000s the government charged the Ministry of Environmental Protection with preparing a policy document on the future of the Dead Sea, centred on an analysis of how the falling level of the sea affects its surroundings. The document set out a series of recommendations to the government on how to act in the region, in the near and the distant future.
items.a03-p006: I headed the team together with several colleagues. At the start of the work we recruited experts from different fields of knowledge. Eli, who knows the Dead Sea and its shores like the back of his hand, was among the first we brought in. Over the course of the work there were discussions, and the members of the team learned <span epub:type="pagebreak" role="doc-pagebreak" id="pg-14" title="10"/>from one another, and we drew up our recommendations to the government. Some of the recommendations contradicted (to put it mildly) the development policy that the leaders of the Tamar Regional Council had prepared. Eli found himself in an awkward position before neighbours and close friends, when he had to confront their view of the world. But he kept to his professional positions and stood by his opinions. At one of the meetings before the position paper was signed, the head of the regional council at the time, Dov Litvinoff, said something that changed the council's attitude – from a hostile document to one whose conclusions had to be adopted for the sake of the sensible development of the region. This is what he said: "Like a mirror set before our faces, it is hard for us to accept the reality reflected before our eyes. A reality we did not know, and one that must be put into practice in planning the future of the region."
items.a03-p007: Geologists characterize a rock by the mixture of minerals that make it up. In my eyes, Eli is a mixture of a triangle of components: the man of the Dead Sea, the geologist of the dolomite plates, and an exacting guide and educator – who lives by the saying: preach well, and practise what you preach! He takes in wide spaces at a glance – but is exacting about the details.
